caption.2:
Everyone says "agent." Almost nobody can tell you where the chatbot ends.

It's three steps on a loop:

PLAN — it decides the steps itself. You give it the job, not the method.
ACT — it uses a real tool. Sends, writes, fetches, books. Not a description of a tool.
CHECK — it looks at what came back, then goes again.

That loop is the entire difference.

One test settles it: if it can't act without you, it's a chatbot with a better name.

And the honest part nobody leads with — agents don't fail like chatbots. A chatbot
gives you a bad answer and you move on. An agent fails confidently, halfway through,
having already done part of the work.

That's why your first one should touch something reversible. A draft, not a send.

out later, when the guess was wrong.

Five real ways this shows up, from agents actually running in production right now.

"If you're not sure, say so — instead of guessing."

That's it. Add it before you trust the output of anything you've built.

Your n8n retry doesn't just try again. It can do the exact same thing twice.

sent. On a retry, check for that key first — if it's already there, stop instead
of sending again. Any external call needs this, not just n8n's own retry.

caption.34:
Your n8n node runs once for every item you send it — not once, total. That's n8n's real model: every node takes in a list of items, and runs its whole logic once per item on that list.

Send an HTTP Request node 40 rows, and it doesn't make one call with 40 rows in it — it makes 40 real calls. That's why a workflow that "ran fine" on a handful of test items can rate-limit without warning, or blow through a bill, the moment it hits 300.

The fix: the Loop Over Items node (officially Split in Batches) groups items before they hit the expensive step. Once you see it as items flowing through one at a time, the whole canvas makes sense.

If that takes more than a few seconds, it looks like the message never arrived — so it gets sent again. n8n has no memory of "I already saw this one." It just runs the entire thing a second time, real actions included.

That's how one real event turns into two real emails, or two real charges — from a system that never once said it failed.

The fix: reply "got it" right when the event arrives, then do the real work next. Nothing sits long enough to be sent twice.

The real, still-current problem is different: ATS software parses a resume into fields (name, dates, job titles, skills) so a person can search and sort it — and real, current formatting choices genuinely break that parsing. Tables and multi-column layouts get read row-by-row and merge into unreadable "word salad." Headers, footers and text boxes are frequently skipped entirely, sometimes dropping name and contact info outright. Photos, icons and skill-bar graphics are invisible to the parser. So a "technically reviewed" application can still reach a recruiter as broken, incomplete data (sourced across multiple 2026 Jobscan/ATS-formatting guides). Recruiters spend roughly 6-10 seconds on that first screen (The Ladders' original 2012 eye-tracking study measured 6 seconds; their 2018 follow-up measured 7.4; current 2025-26 surveys put 42% of HR professionals under 10 seconds) — nowhere near enough time to notice information is missing and go looking for it.

The fix that actually works, free, right now:
— One column, not a designed template
— Plain section titles: Experience, Education, Skills
— The exact language from the job posting
— Send it as a real .docx or a text-layer PDF — never a flattened image
